slot.brief: Definite integral of a rational function in sin/cos or a rational function requiring substitution and symmetry; moderate simplification.

stem: The value of the definite integral from 0 to pi of x sin(x) divided by (1 + cos^2(x)) with respect to x is:

verdicts.working: Let f(x)=sin x/(1+cos²x), so f(π−x)=f(x). Hence 2I=π∫₀^π f(x)dx. With u=cos x, ∫₀^π f(x)dx=∫₋₁¹ du/(1+u²)=π/2. Thus I=π²/4.

working:
Let I = integral from 0 to pi of x sin x/(1+cos^2 x) dx. Replace x by pi-x: I = integral from 0 to pi of (pi-x) sin x/(1+cos^2 x) dx. Adding gives 2I = pi * integral from 0 to pi of sin x/(1+cos^2 x) dx. Put cos x = t, so -sin x dx = dt. The remaining integral becomes integral from -1 to 1 of dt/(1+t^2) = pi/2. Thus 2I = pi*(pi/2), so I = pi^2/4.

Independent check: Let f(x)=sin x/(1+cos²x), so f(π−x)=f(x). Hence 2I=π∫₀^π f(x)dx. With u=cos x, ∫₀^π f(x)dx=∫₋₁¹ du/(1+u²)=π/2. Thus I=π²/4.
solution:
Let $I=\int_0^\pi \frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x}\,dx$. Replacing $x$ by $\pi-x$ and adding, using symmetry of $\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x}$, gives
$$2I=\pi\int_0^\pi \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x}\,dx=\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{2},$$
where $u=\cos x$. Hence $I=\boxed{\frac{\pi^2}{4}}$.
